title: The fall from the horse
hookLine: thrown and nearly killed, Montaigne found dying felt soft and dreamy, not terrible (Essays 2.6)

cards: An easy ride, not far from home, in a time of civil war. Montaigne is on a gentle horse that isn't very strong, with his men around him.

One of them, a big, sturdy fellow on a powerful horse, wants to show off his nerve and get ahead of the others. He spurs hard, comes up behind at full speed, and crashes straight into his master. Man and horse go down.
Montaigne lands far off, flat on his back, and doesn't move.

teach.b: First, the fall. Montaigne tells it himself in the essay Of Practice. He lies there stunned, bloody, his sword flung away, and his companions think he's dead.
They carry him home with great trouble. On the way he starts to breathe and stir, and he throws up blood. Second, the surprise.
What was it like inside? Not terror.
His life seemed to be hanging on the edge of his lips, he says, and he closed his eyes as if to help push it out, and found a kind of pleasure in letting go, like drifting off to sleep.
The feeling wasn't only free of distress; it had a sweetness in it. He wonders whether people we see thrashing near death are as far away inside as he was. Third, the return.
Later, when his memory really returned, the whole fall came back at once, like a lightning strike, and only then did it feel like dying.

teach.h: PRACTICE FOR WHAT CAN'T BE PRACTICED.
teach.b: Death, he says, is something we can't rehearse; when it comes, we're all beginners. But we can get close and look. This fall was the nearest he'd come, so he studied it.
And he says plainly that this is his own study, not a lesson for anyone else. He doesn't promise anyone a soft ending.
He reports what his was like: the moment itself was gentler than the coming back.

how: Readers of Montaigne often return to this essay when they're afraid of dying: not as a promise, but as one man's careful report of how close he came and what it was like.

games.q: what does “the fall from the horse” mean?
o: a knight's disgrace after losing a well-known jousting match
the day Montaigne gave up riding and stayed in his tower
Montaigne's near-death fall: soft inside, hard coming back

p: wanted to show off his nerve
his own study, not a lesson

s: Montaigne says the moment near death was full of terror
he says it was free of distress, with a kind of sweetness, like falling asleep.
his companions thought he was dead
they carried him home with great trouble, and he began to breathe on the way.
he says everyone's death will feel soft
he says what he writes is his own study, not a lesson for others; it's a report, not a promise.

games.q: you're Montaigne, lying in the road after the crash, your life seeming to hang on your lips. what do you feel?
o: panic, and a fight to stay alive.
nothing; and later you remember none of it.
games.why: he says he closed his eyes and found pleasure in letting go, like drifting off to sleep. the pain came later, when memory returned like lightning.

practice: If you're willing, bring back a near miss of your own, a swerve on the highway or a scary wait for news; if that's too heavy, choose a smaller one, or just stay with the breath.
Notice the fear before, the moment itself and the shock after, and which was heaviest, then rest.
If thoughts of death feel heavy in a darker way, you don't have to carry them alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: The fall from the horse. Thrown and left for dead, Montaigne found the moment near death soft, like falling asleep; the coming back and the memory were harder. Today's word.

orig.note: French, the essay's title: of practice, of exercising yourself for something.

carryVoice: Your line: softer than feared. Sometimes the dread weighs more than the thing itself. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Essays 2.6, Of Practice (De l'exercitation): the collision with a servant on a strong horse; left for dead and carried home; life hanging at his lips, a pleasant letting go like sleep; the memory returning like lightning; death cannot be rehearsed, but approached; his study, not a lesson for others
